newsitem.title: USA: Whistleblowers say tobacco pact should be toughened.
newsitem.headline: Whistleblowers say tobacco pact should be toughened.

text.p: A group of tobacco industry "whistleblowers" on Friday urged revision of a $368.5 billion settlement, saying the industry should be made to disclose more fully its information on cigarettes and nicotine.

"I don't feel the agreement is an acceptable one ... I'm not sure why we're rushing so much," former Philip Morris scientist Victor DeNoble said after a meeting at the White House. "Why do we have to come to an agreement today and simply take money from the industry?" he added.

The meeting, chaired by Vice President Al Gore, was part of a presidential task force review of the wide-ranging settlement worked out last month between the tobacco industry and state attorneys general.

Asked what he would regard as a good agreement, DeNoble said: "Regulation by the Food and Drug Administration. The creation of a combined body ... to make a safer product ... A real commitment to changing the way the tobacco product is made would begin to make a good agreement."

Jeffrey Wigand, a former vice president of research and development for Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., and former Philip Morris Cos. Inc. scientists Paul Mele and Ian Uydess were also present. All generally agreed that the pact should be revised.

Mele said the tobacco industry had a "tremendous supply of data" on the health consequences of smoking and that this data should be fully disclosed "if this industry is going to reinvent itself in a more acceptable fashion."
"I think the major message of today ... was that we need a lot of document disclosure," Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala, who also attended the meeting, told reporters afterwards.
"We need to know a lot and, therefore, the document disclosure part of the settlement ... is something that we need to look at very carefully."
President Bill Clinton's domestic policy adviser Bruce Reed added: "We learned a great deal about nicotine and what the industry may or may not know about developing reduced-risk cigarettes."
The Washington Post said on Friday that tobacco industry representatives had warned that the settlement could fall apart if Congress and the White House dallied over changes.

It quoted these individuals as saying that the provision that limits the Food and Drug Administration's ability to regulate nicotine, which Clinton has labeled "unreasonable," was critical to the industry.
But Shalala scoffed at the industry threats to walk away from the settlement, terming them predictable posturing.
"I think this is what people do when they want a deal. They talk tough ... There's just a lot of dancing around that takes place," she said.
